question: A 70-year-old man with NYHA class III heart failure is listed for elective cholecystectomy. Which perioperative principle is most important before proceeding?

answers.text: Proceed immediately — delaying elective surgery increases the risk of acute cholecystitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Risk stratification must precede any elective procedure; operating on an unoptimised patient with severe cardiac disease significantly increases perioperative mortality.

answers.text: Optimise the cardiac condition and reassess operative risk before proceeding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Risk stratification identifies high-risk patients, and optimisation — here of cardiac function — is the key preoperative principle before any elective procedure.

answers.text: Convert to laparoscopic approach to reduce anaesthetic time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Technique modification may be part of the plan, but cannot substitute for cardiac optimisation and risk reassessment in a class III heart failure patient.

answers.text: Obtain written consent and proceed — the patient has autonomy to accept the risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Patient autonomy does not remove the surgical team's obligation to optimise modifiable risk. Consent cannot substitute for clinical risk management.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the perioperative principles: risk stratification → optimisation → safety systems. For a patient with NYHA class III heart failure, optimisation of cardiac function is non-negotiable before elective surgery.
Well done. Risk stratification followed by optimisation of modifiable comorbidities is the first perioperative principle, and is mandatory before any elective procedure in a high-risk patient.
